system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker HOT_KRAS (KRAS hotspot mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking:
KRAS looks like the clear primary target, since all 84 altered lines depend on it strongly and the pattern holds across lineages, though it's already well established. RAF1 comes next with a weaker 38% dependence, concentrated in pancreas, biliary and lymphoid lines and not in lung. I'll register KRAS as the primary and replicate it, and perhaps RAF1 as a secondary too.

I'm going to register both KRAS and RAF1 and replicate each of them, with the replication budget at five.

input.mechanism: Oncogenic KRAS hotspot mutants (G12/G13/Q61) are GTP-locked and drive MAPK/PI3K signalling; mutant-allele lines become addicted to continued KRAS expression (oncogene addiction), so knockout of KRAS is more lethal in mutant lines than in KRAS wild-type lines.

Mutant KRAS signals to MAPK largely through RAF dimers; RAF1 (CRAF) is required in some KRAS-mutant contexts (paradoxical/dimer-dependent signalling), giving a partial selective dependence in a subset of KRAS-mutant lines (pancreatic, biliary, lymphoid).

findings.claim: HOT_KRAS-mutant cancer lines depend strongly on KRAS itself (all 84 discovery lines strongly dependent, mean effect -1.99 vs -0.62 in others; lineage-adjusted beta -1.23); this held in 71 held-out Broad lines (p=2.4e-51) and 41 independent Sanger-screen altered lines (p=7e-18). It is the oncogene-addiction dependency, not a novel finding, and KRAS is also broadly essential so the therapeutic window is mostly defined by mutant-vs-WT differential effect, not absolute lethality.

RAF1 shows a weaker, lineage-dependent dependence in KRAS-mutant lines (discovery beta -0.26); it replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-8) but not in the independent Sanger screen (p=0.045, above threshold), so it is not a robust selective target.

input.summary: Best candidate for HOT_KRAS populations is KRAS itself. Its dependency is the strongest and most consistent signal in the data: essentially every KRAS-hotspot line is strongly dependent on KRAS versus only about half of wild-type lines, and this replicated in held-out Broad lines and an independent Sanger screen. This is a well-established oncogene-addiction dependency rather than a new discovery; the translational challenge is that KRAS is broadly essential, so selectivity rests on the mutant-vs-WT difference (about -1.2 effect units) rather than absolute lethality. The secondary candidate RAF1 was weaker, lineage-driven (pancreatic, biliary, lymphoid), and failed replication in the Sanger screen. Other lower-ranked hits (MAP3K2, CFLAR, ILK) were not tested and are weak or broadly essential.
